description: Time da UFU (Sistemas de Informação) participando do desafio Field Shift. Vamos usar dados da NASA pra criar uma solução que ajude fazendas a se adaptarem, com foco em entregar uma demo que funcione.
summary: AgroAI is a free, mobile-first website, in English and Portuguese, that helps small and mid-size farmers in Brazil and the United States choose healthier crop rotations with NASA data. The farmer marks the farm on a map and answers a short questionnaire about current crops and planting months, what they know about the soil and their priorities: save water, improve the soil, prevent erosion, fewer pests, extra income or animal feed. AgroAI combines NASA POWER climate and SRTM slope with SoilGrids soil data and a sourced crop catalog, and compares the current rotation with the two best alternatives. For each one it explains why, the evidence, benefits, risks, confidence and information gaps, exactly what the Field Shift challenge asks for. A dashboard adds live SMAP soil moisture, MODIS NDVI and GPM IMERG rain, and a chat assistant answers questions in plain language, citing the source of every number. AgroAI supports and does not decide: scores come from transparent rules, the AI never computes or invents a number, and the final word belongs to the farmer.
details:
Live app: https://agroai.mateusmoreira.dev

Demo version (sample farm in Iowa, log in with just a name, "Skip All" on the questionnaire): https://demo-agroai.mateusmoreira.dev

Source code: https://github.com/eeomts/FieldShift-NasaSpaceApps-Hackathon

WHAT IT DOES

Changing weather, irregular rain, water shortage and worn-out soil make it hard to decide what to plant and when. AgroAI turns decades of free NASA data into a crop-rotation comparison a farmer can act on this season. It shows the months when the field is bare, the seasons when the current crops are more vulnerable (frost during flowering, water deficit, heavy rain on bare soil), and rotation options that fill those gaps.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Questionnaire: the farmer marks the farm on a map and describes, in their own words, what they plant and when. They also answer about soil observations (with reference photos), equipment, irrigation and up to 3 priorities. "I don't know" is always accepted. The questions adapt to the local climate zone (Köppen, computed from NASA POWER), so frost questions don't show up in the tropics.

2. Data: from the location, the back-end reads NASA POWER (daily data and 1991-2020 normals), SRTM slope, SoilGrids soil properties and a 7-day Open-Meteo forecast. The dashboard also reads recent SMAP L4 soil moisture, MODIS NDVI and GPM IMERG rain live from NASA Earthdata.

3. Soil portrait: it merges lab results, field tests, the farmer's observations and SoilGrids, each with a confidence weight. When sources disagree, the app says so.

4. Rotation engine: it generates candidates (fill the bare window, swap for a drought-tolerant crop, add a legume) and removes the ones that don't fit (growing degree days, frost during flowering, missing equipment, crops the farmer won't grow). Each remaining option gets a score from 0 to 1 on 6 criteria: water, soil, erosion, pests, income and animal feed. Water demand follows FAO-56 (ET0 computed from NASA POWER, ETc = Kc x ET0). Erosion uses rainfall, SRTM slope and soil erodibility (USLE K). The farmer's priorities weight the final score.

5. Results: the current rotation next to the 2 best alternatives, each with why, evidence, risks, confidence and gaps, plus a "where this came from" view of every number. A chat assistant that knows the farm explains the results in plain language.

BENEFITS

Free NASA data becomes plain-language guidance on the phone, in two languages, with metric or imperial units depending on the country. Every recommendation can be explained and traced to its source and period. Farmers without a soil test still get an analysis, and the farmer's own knowledge counts.

INTENDED IMPACT

Help small and mid-size farmers adopt rotations that keep the soil covered, reduce erosion and water stress and add income. Give agronomists and extension services a transparent tool they can check and adapt. Next steps: official planting windows (ZARC in Brazil, USDA NASS in the US), local market data, bringing SMAP, NDVI and IMERG into the analysis and the chat, and validation with extension services.

TOOLS

Back-end: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, Pydantic, pytest (more than 800 automated tests). Database: PostgreSQL with pgvector. Front-end: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet. Infrastructure: Docker and Caddy on a VPS. AI: Google Gemini, for language tasks only (reading free-text answers, the chat and knowledge-base search). The code was written with help from Claude Code. No special hardware.

CREATIVE ASPECT

- The farmer describes the farm in their own words, and the app turns it into a crop calendar matched to a sourced catalog.

- Soil is a portrait built from several pieces of evidence, each with its own confidence, not one number from a global map.

- The AI never computes or invents a number: every number comes from NASA data, the catalog or a formula in code, and is shown with its source.

- Strict rules can remove a strategy, but the app always explains why.

- The result is a comparison, not an order: it shows confidence and information gaps next to each strategy.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Farmers with weak internet and only a phone: mobile-first screens, short questions, simple language.

- Different levels of soil knowledge: three data profiles (experience, observer, lab report), and "I don't know" is always valid.

- Honest limits of the data: NASA POWER cells are about 50 km wide and the app says so. Each number shows its scale and period, and each source shows its license.

- Trust: the tool supports and does not decide, and every screen reminds the farmer to confirm with a local expert.

- Privacy and cost: the farmer can delete the account and all farm data, and everything runs on free data sources.
